Before the First World War, Europe was divided into two rival power blocs. Alliances were intended to protect countries, but they also connected separate disputes and increased suspicion between the major powers.

## The two blocs

The **Triple Alliance** consisted of:

- Germany
- Austria-Hungary
- Italy

The opposing **Triple Entente** linked:

- Britain
- France
- Russia

An entente was an understanding rather than exactly the same kind of formal military alliance. However, both groupings encouraged governments to expect support from friendly powers and to prepare for conflict with the rival bloc.

Several tensions reinforced this division. France resented Germany after losing Alsace-Lorraine in an earlier war. Germany’s growing military and naval strength worried Britain. Austria-Hungary and Russia competed for influence in the Balkans. These disputes made the alliances feel increasingly necessary, while the alliances themselves deepened fear and military planning.

## How the danger grew

A cause map can show the relationship:

$$\\text{existing tensions} \\rightarrow \\text{rival alliances} \\rightarrow \\text{greater suspicion and wider war risk}$$

For example, a confrontation involving Austria-Hungary and Russia would not necessarily remain a dispute between two empires. Germany might support Austria-Hungary, while France might support Russia. Britain could then become involved alongside France and Russia. Alliances therefore created a route by which a local crisis could spread across Europe.

A common mix-up is to say that alliances alone caused the war. They did not automatically produce conflict. Instead, they divided Europe and made an existing crisis more likely to expand into a general war." Expected: /prewar|before (?:1914|World War I)/i
